chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Barqi, from Aban al-Ahmar, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn al-Khazzaz, from Harun ibn Harizah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

We were with him, and we mentioned al-Husayn (peace be upon him) – may Allah's curse be upon his killers. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) wept, and we wept with him. He said, then he raised his head and said: Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said, 'I am the Martyr of Tears; no believer remembers me without weeping.'

key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdillah, a title for Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)
key_terms.الْحُسَيْنُ (ع): Imam al-Husayn, the third Shia Imam, grandson of the Prophet
key_terms.قَتِيلُ الْعَبْرَةِ: Martyr of Tears, a title for Imam al-Husayn referring to his weeping martyrdom
key_terms.لَعْنَةُ اللَّهِ: The curse of Allah, invoking divine displeasure upon his killers

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of Imam al-Husayn being called the 'Martyr of Tears' in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Kamil al-Ziyarat* establishes the theological link between remembrance (dhikr) and emotional response (buka'), framing Imam al-Husayn’s martyrdom as a catalyst for spiritual awakening among believers. It underscores the Shia concept of 'Al-Abrah' (the weeping), where tears serve as a tangible sign of faith and connection to the Ahl al-Bayt, a tradition deeply rooted in the practices of the Imams.
